stories.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.
